Our World: The week of Oct. 26, 2026
Our World is a roundup from our weekly print edition of noteworthy happenings, from our global correspondents and editors.
A pay-for-citizenship plan in Argentina
Argentina has become one of the first Group of 20 countries to move toward a “golden passport” program. A proposal unveiled by the government in early October says that in exchange for payments of $350,000 for a principal applicant or a bond purchase of $800,000, foreigners can become eligible for citizenship. Golden passports and visas have typically been favored by smaller nations struggling to attract foreign investment, such as Portugal and Saint Kitts. The program has not gone before Argentina’s congress, but ahead of next year’s presidential election, President Javier Milei’s opposition is already speaking out, calling the program elitist. – Whitney Eulich    
China’s AI chip boom
China’s chipmakers are benefiting from a boom in demand as a result of export controls on U.S. semiconductors. Firms such as Huawei and Alibaba are finding it’s a seller’s market, as year-over-year demand was up more than 400% in the first quarter, according to the financial media outlet Caixin. A chip shortage has held back some leading Chinese AI model developers, causing them to pause adding new subscribers this spring and summer. But the Chinese chip firms also face manufacturing bottlenecks, which are expected to persist in the coming two years, Caixin reports. – Ann Scott Tyson    
In this week’s roundup from our international team: Argentina unveils a “golden passport” program, China’s chipmakers see a boom in demand, preaching on Ghana’s long-distance buses is now illegal, and Greenland debates the future of the world’s slowest sharks.
“Not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday.”
That’s Boateng Bismark James, explaining to the BBC why he preaches on Ghana’s long-distance buses. Such pastors are a common sight in the West African country, pacing the aisles as they deliver sermons that can last for hours. But enforcement recently began for a law passed in May that makes the practice illegal, categorizing it as a nuisance that affects the safety and comfort of travelers. Public opinion is divided. Mr. James makes his income through contributions from passengers grateful for the service. Others say they prefer peace and quiet en route to their destinations.  – Ryan Lenora Brown  
Greenland debates future of shark species
A plan to cull 1,000 Greenland sharks has been dropped after questions about its legality. But, the Guardian reports, the prospect of a future cull still exists. Trawlers that fish off Greenland’s coast are having to compete for halibut and cod with Greenland sharks – the slowest sharks in the world and the second-largest carnivorous fish species. Conservationists say a cull wouldn’t work because other sharks would simply move into the area. They point to other issues that need to be addressed, such as too many boats and no alternative employment for fishers.  –Tim Backshall
